disclaimer: This is an automated check of a paper's reported numbers and its internal record -- not a finding of misconduct. It is NOT adequate for definitive detection of wrongdoing or fraud.
paper_title: RETRACTED ARTICLE: Happiness as alchemy: Positive mood leads to self-serving responses to social comparisons

paper_metadata.authors: Camille S. Johnson, Diederik A. Stapel
paper_metadata.study_design: Four between-subjects factorial laboratory experiments plus a pilot study; mood manipulated by autobiographical essay, social-comparison direction and similarity-cue ambiguity manipulated between subjects. NOTE: the article is published as RETRACTED (title carries the retraction marker); the second author is Diederik Stapel, whose work was retracted en masse following the 2011 Levelt/Noort/Drenth investigations. This review evaluates the printed numbers on their own terms and does not rely on the retraction for any finding.

hypotheses.statement: In a positive mood, an ambiguous similarity cue (shared birthday) permits asymmetric, self-serving responding: assimilation to upward comparison targets and contrast away from downward targets; with no such cue, responding is symmetric.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Ambiguous similarity information was expected to allow for asymmetric and self-serving responses: assimilation to upward comparison targets and contrast with downward targets.

hypotheses.statement: Negative mood does not produce asymmetric self-serving responding, ruling out a mood-congruency account; positive mood does.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: If asymmetric interpretations result from mood-congruent processing, negative mood should be associated with asymmetrically self-harming interpretations.

hypotheses.statement: Self-serving responding occurs only when the similarity information is explicitly ambiguous; when it is described as unambiguous, positive and neutral mood respond alike.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: asymmetry in responding was only expected when the similarity cue was described as ambiguous.

hypotheses.statement: Self-serving reinterpretation in a positive mood is effortful and therefore eliminated by cognitive load.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: asymmetric responding in a positive mood results from effortful reinterpretation of ambiguous information

findings.location: Experiment 4, No load conditions and Cognitive load conditions (control-condition statistics, repeated twice)
findings.quote: Higher levels of self-evaluations relative to the control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21) were found

computed.explanation_at_n15: total 63: no integer sum-of-squares Q with the required parity falls in the window [265.19, 265.25] implied by SD=0.21 at 2 dp

consequence.explanation: This control mean and SD is the reference point against which all eight of Experiment 4's self-evaluation contrasts are tested, so the impossibility sits under the whole of the paper's cognitive-load conclusion.

findings.notes: The self-evaluation measure is a single seven-point integer item, so the observations must be whole numbers. With a mean of exactly 4.20, at least a fifth of responses must depart from 4, which forces a sample SD of roughly 0.41 or more; 0.21 is below the floor. Verified independently by R's rsprite2 (infeasible=true), and robust to the unknown control-group size: no integer sample exists at n = 15, 20, 30 or 60. n=15 is the value implied by the reported degrees of freedom. Value confirmed identically in both the XML and the PDF version of record.

findings.location: Experiment 3, Manipulation check
findings.quote: the upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 7.33, SD = 1.19) than the downward target (M = 4.17, SD = 1.19), F(1,88) = 170.34, p < .001

consequence.explanation: The affected claim is Experiment 3's direction-of-comparison manipulation check, which licenses the interpretation of the entire experiment as an upward-versus-downward comparison.

findings.notes: Experiment 3 states its attractiveness ratings used 'the seam [same] measures used in Experiments 1 and 2', both of which explicitly define a seven-point scale (1 = not at all attractive, 7 = extremely attractive). A mean of 7.33 exceeds that maximum and is unattainable at any n. The bound is stated by the paper via explicit cross-reference rather than assumed by me. Either the mean is wrong or the methods description of the scale is wrong; a nine-point scale would reconcile 7.33 and 4.17 around a midpoint of 5, but the paper does not say that. Note also that the same value 7.33 is reported in the same paragraph as the positive-mood mean, and both attractiveness SDs are identically 1.19.

consequence.explanation: None of the three inconsistencies crosses alpha, so no reported conclusion changes; all three affected results are non-significant or already significant either way. Computed from 0 statistic(s) whose recomputed p crosses the paper's alpha.

findings.notes: 3 of 65 is a low rate and is unremarkable on its own -- roughly half of clean control papers contain at least one such mismatch. Two have benign explanations: the pilot's F(1,42) is almost certainly a typo for F(2,42), since the design has three groups and F(2,42)=0.27 gives p=.757, matching the printed .76 (this is corroborated below by rivets_anova); and p=.83 for F=1.50 may be a transposition of .23. findings.location: Experiment 2, Manipulation check
findings.quote: The upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 5.98, SD = .69) than the downward target (M = 2.46, SD = .74), F(1,118) = 716.92, p < .001.

consequence.explanation: No claim is affected; the manipulation check is significant under either value by an enormous margin.

findings.notes: Downgraded from the tool's highly_suspicious to indeterminate, deliberately. The tool recomputes a ONE-WAY ANOVA, but the paper's F carries df_error=118, i.e. it comes from the residual of the full 2x2x2 model. The one-way error term uses df=124; moving six further effects (all reported as Fs<1) out of the residual raises the mean square and lowers F by roughly the ratio 124/118, which brings the expected value to about 725 -- close to the printed 716.92. The apparent discrepancy is therefore largely explained by the model I could fit versus the model they fitted, and I am not treating it as evidence against the paper. The same caveat does not apply to the pilot ANOVA, which really is one-way.

severity_source.note: The tool returned `highly_suspicious`; this finding records `indeterminate`. A reason is stated in the finding.

findings.quote: Exposure to the upward comparison target led to lowered self-evaluations (M = 3.33, SD = .65) compared to the downward comparison target (M = 4.64, SD = 1.50), F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011.

inputs.comparison: simple-effect df against the omnibus 2x2 ANOVA df in the same analysis

consequence.explanation: Affects the simple-effect test carrying Experiment 1's symmetric-contrast claim in the different-birthday condition; p is .011 under either df, so the conclusion is unchanged.

findings.notes: Every other test in Experiment 1 uses df_error=43, correct for N=47 in a 2x2 design. This one simple effect uses 46, which is N-1 and corresponds to no error term in the stated design. The p-value is unaffected (F(1,46)=6.95 gives p=.0114; F(1,43)=6.95 gives p=.0116, both printing as .011), so this is a reporting inconsistency rather than a computational one.
findings.reproduction: Not reproducible as a CLI command: this compares two printed degrees-of-freedom values against the stated design, which no forensic tool evaluates.

findings.location: Experiment 3, footnote 4
findings.quote: Complete data and results available from the first author.

inputs.comparison: the paper's data-availability statement against the material actually supplied

consequence.explanation: Every impossibility recorded above could be resolved or refuted immediately by the raw data the footnote offers; none of it is deposited.

findings.notes: A state-but-withhold data-availability claim (rulebook rule 7): the paper asserts complete data are available but deposits nothing, and the offer is attached to a single footnote in one experiment rather than to the paper as a whole. This co-occurs with two dependent measures named in Table 1's caption that are never reported (see table1_caption_promises_absent_rows). Recorded as suspicious, in the specific sense that the claim cannot be acted on, not as evidence of intent.
findings.reproduction: Not reproducible as a CLI command: this records the presence of a data-availability claim and the absence of deposited data, which no forensic tool evaluates.

findings.location: Experiment 3 Manipulation check; Table 2 Similarity row
findings.quote: the upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 7.33, SD = 1.19) than the downward target (M = 4.17, SD = 1.19) | Similarity ... 6.81 (1.16) 6.81 (.63)

inputs.comparison: printed values within Experiment 3 and within the pilot

consequence.explanation: No claim depends on this; it is recorded as a weak corroborating pattern only.

findings.notes: Three coincidences of repeated values, each individually unremarkable: two attractiveness SDs identical at 1.19 in the same sentence; two similarity means identical at 6.81 in adjacent Table 2 cells; two pilot self-evaluation means identical at 6.98. Rulebook rule 8 -- individually weak signals, reported but not escalated. They are noted because they co-occur with the impossibility findings, and because the SD pair 1.19/1.19 sits in the same sentence as the out-of-range mean 7.33. Recorded as indeterminate: repeated values are ordinary in small samples and prove nothing on their own.
findings.reproduction: Not reproducible as a CLI command: detect_duplication (see duplication_sweep) found no identical (mean, SD) pairs; these are repeats of a single component, which that tool does not flag.

unchecked.reason: check_table refused GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE on all 8 cells: the similarity index is a mean of three 9-point items, so it moves in steps of 1/(3n) rather than 1/n, and grim_test has no items parameter. Running the granularity check with 1/n would manufacture impossibilities. Hand-checking the 1/36 granularity would be unvalidated arithmetic, so these cells are recorded as unchecked rather than checked by an improvised method.

unchecked.location: Pilot study mood and self-evaluation means (six values)
unchecked.reason: Both are means of multi-item composites (4 nine-point items and 3 nine-point items), so GRIM/GRIMMER do not apply for the same granularity reason. The ANOVAs computed from them were checked with rivets_anova instead.

Neither figure carries values absent from the text: Figure 2 replots Table 2's self-evaluation row and Figure 3 replots Experiment 4's prose cell means, all of which were checked directly. No error-bar meaning is stated in either caption, so no dispersion could have been read off them in any case, and figure-derived values are barred from the exact-arithmetic checks that produced this review's findings.

unchecked.location: Experiment 2 contrast tests reported with df_error=124 (four tests)
unchecked.reason: The error df of 124 corresponds to neither the factorial model (118) nor the contrast model (132) used elsewhere in the same experiment. Without knowing which sub-model produced it I could not reconstruct the group sizes, so these F values were left unverified rather than checked against a guessed model.

The paper prints no cell sizes anywhere. Every n used in this review was derived from reported degrees of freedom and the stated design; where two candidate sizes were possible I ran the check at both and reported only results that failed under both. Findings resting on a derived n are graded highly_suspicious rather than impossible for that reason.

None were provided with the paper. The article's footnote 4 states 'Complete data and results available from the first author', but no data file accompanies the record, so nothing could be read. This is 'not provided', distinct from 'present but unreadable'.

check_effect_plausibility was not run. The paper reports no effect sizes and no dispersion for several key contrasts, and the group statistics that do exist are themselves the object of the impossibility findings above; benchmarking a d computed from values that cannot be produced by any integer sample would not be informative.
